title: Are there infinitely many primes of the form n^2 + 1?
rootQuestion: Are there infinitely many primes of the form n^2 + 1?

workingPaperSections.title: Examples and finite checks
workingPaperSections.body:
Research workstream: Small examples and counterexamples

Computation:
- Command: python3 search.py
- Exit code: 0
- Runtime: 68ms

Findings:
- The computation checked \[ 1\le n\le 100 \]
- with exit code \(0\) and runtime about \(68\) ms.
- Prime-producing values found: \[ n=1,2,4,6,10,14,16,20,24,26,36,40,54,56,66,74,84,90,94. \]
- Thus, in this finite range, \(19\) out of \(100\) tested values gave prime \(n^2+1\).
- Elementary theorem-level observations:
- If \(n>1\) is odd, then \(n^2+1\) is even and greater than \(2\), hence composite.
- If an odd prime \(p\mid n^2+1\), then \[ n^2\equiv -1\pmod p, \] so \(-1\) is a quadratic residue mod \(p\). Therefore \[ p\equiv 1\pmod 4. \] Finite observed least prime divisors among composites included: \[ 2,5,13,17,29,37,41,53,73, \] all odd ones congruent to \(1\bmod 4\), consistent with the theorem above.

Limitations:
- This search is finite and only covers \(1\le n\le 100\). It gives no proof that infinitely many primes of the form \(n^2+1\) exist.
- The statistic \(19/100\) is only a bounded observation and should not be interpreted as an asymptotic density.
- The divisor table records only least prime divisors, not complete factorizations.
- The observed residue classes are empirical least-divisor patterns, not a full modular analysis.
- A finite computation does not prove an infinite claim.

Open gaps:
- The root question remains open: it is not known unconditionally whether there are infinitely many primes of the form \[ n^2+1. \]
- The computation provides examples and confirms basic modular constraints, but it does not address arbitrarily large \(n\).
- No mechanism is shown that forces new prime values of \(n^2+1\) to occur indefinitely.

Next: Extend computations to larger \(n\), while still treating them as finite evidence only. Record full factorizations, not just least prime divisors. Compare observed counts with Bateman–Horn heuristic predictions.

workingPaperSections.body:
Project coordinator synthesis

What we know:
- If \(n>1\) is odd, then \(n^2+1\equiv 2\pmod 4\), hence composite.
- Thus all nontrivial prime examples require \(n\) even.
- If an odd prime \(p\mid n^2+1\), then \(-1\) is a quadratic residue mod \(p\), so \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\).
- Finite computation checked \(1\le n\le 100\). Prime-producing values were \[ n=1,2,4,6,10,14,16,20,24,26,36,40,54,56,66,74,84,90,94. \] This is finite evidence only, not proof of infinitude.
- [source-2] proves related multivariable results, e.g. \[ X^2+(Y^2+1)^2,\qquad X^2+(Y^3+Z^3)^2, \] but these do not imply infinitely many primes \(n^2+1\).
- [source-5] directly concerns quadratic progressions, but is recorded only as a proposed/preprint-style claim, not settled proof.

Current roadblocks:
- No saved report gives a complete proof of infinitely many primes \(n^2+1\).
- The claim that this is a standard open problem is recorded as plausible but not source-backed by the supplied sources.
- Multivariable prime-producing theorems have already been rejected as direct routes; do not specialize variables unless a theorem explicitly permits it.
- General infinitude of primes is not evidence for infinitude inside \(n^2+1\).
- Current computation is bounded and cannot prove an infinite claim.

latestFindings: If an odd prime \(p\mid n^2+1\), then \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\).

details: Convention: \(f(n)=n^2+1\), \(n\in\mathbb Z\). A finite-prime-set covering obstruction means a finite set \(S\) of primes such that for every \(n\), some \(p\in S\) divides \(f(n)\).

**Divisor condition.** If \(p\) is an odd prime and \(p\mid n^2+1\), then \[ n^2\equiv -1 \pmod p. \] Hence \(n^{p-1}\equiv (-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p\). By Fermat, if \(p\nmid n\), then \(n^{p-1}\equiv 1\pmod p\). Therefore \[ (-1)^{(p-1)/2}=1, \] so \((p-1)/2\) is even and \[ p\equiv 1 \pmod 4. \] Thus no odd prime \(p\equiv 3\pmod 4\) can divide any value \(n^2+1\).

Conversely, if \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\), then \(-1\) is a quadratic residue mod \(p\), so the congruence \[ n^2+1\equiv 0\pmod p \] has exactly two residue-class solutions modulo \(p\). For \(p=2\), it has exactly one solution: \(n\equiv 1\pmod 2\).

**No finite-prime-set covering obstruction.** Let \(S\) be any finite set of primes. Choose \[ n\equiv 0\pmod p \] for every \(p\in S\), equivalently \(n\) is a multiple of \(\prod_{p\in S}p\). Then for every \(p\in S\), \[ n^2+1\equiv 1\pmod p, \] so no prime in \(S\) divides \(n^2+1\). Therefore no finite set of primes can cover all values of \(n^2+1\).
The polynomial \(n^2+1\) is locally admissible in the basic sense: for every prime \(p\), there exists a residue class \(n\bmod p\) such that \(p\nmid n^2+1\).
More strongly, any finite set of primes can be avoided simultaneously by the simple CRT-compatible choice \(n\equiv 0\pmod p\) for all \(p\in S\).
These facts do **not** prove infinitely many primes of the form \(n^2+1\).
They only rule out finite local congruence obstructions.
A Euclid-style argument can force new prime divisors of some \(n^2+1\), but not that \(n^2+1\) itself is prime.
Seek a mechanism stronger than admissibility: one would need control over compositeness of \(n^2+1\), not merely over its prime divisors.
Any direct proof must bridge the gap between “values avoid every fixed finite set of primes” and “infinitely many values have no nontrivial prime divisor.”

incrementalReports.title: Specialist attempt
details: Convention: \(f(n)=n^2+1\), \(n\in\mathbb Z\). A finite-prime-set covering obstruction means a finite set \(S\) of primes such that for every \(n\), some \(p\in S\) divides \(f(n)\).

**Divisor condition.** If \(p\) is an odd prime and \(p\mid n^2+1\), then \[ n^2\equiv -1 \pmod p. \] Hence \(n^{p-1}\equiv (-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p\). By Fermat, if \(p\nmid n\), then \(n^{p-1}\equiv 1\pmod p\). Therefore \[ (-1)^{(p-1)/2}=1, \] so \((p-1)/2\) is even and \[ p\equiv 1 \pmod 4. \] Thus no odd prime \(p\equiv 3\pmod 4\) can divide any value \(n^2+1\).

Conversely, if \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\), then \(-1\) is a quadratic residue mod \(p\), so the congruence \[ n^2+1\equiv 0\pmod p \] has exactly two residue-class solutions modulo \(p\). For \(p=2\), it has exactly one solution: \(n\equiv 1\pmod 2\).

**No finite-prime-set covering obstruction.** Let \(S\) be any finite set of primes. Choose \[ n\equiv 0\pmod p \] for every \(p\in S\), equivalently \(n\) is a multiple of \(\prod_{p\in S}p\). Then for every \(p\in S\), \[ n^2+1\equiv 1\pmod p, \] so no prime in \(S\) divides \(n^2+1\). Therefore no finite set of primes can cover all values of \(n^2+1\).
The polynomial \(n^2+1\) is locally admissible in the basic sense: for every prime \(p\), there exists a residue class \(n\bmod p\) such that \(p\nmid n^2+1\).
More strongly, any finite set of primes can be avoided simultaneously by the simple CRT-compatible choice \(n\equiv 0\pmod p\) for all \(p\in S\).
These facts do **not** prove infinitely many primes of the form \(n^2+1\).
They only rule out finite local congruence obstructions.
A Euclid-style argument can force new prime divisors of some \(n^2+1\), but not that \(n^2+1\) itself is prime.
Seek a mechanism stronger than admissibility: one would need control over compositeness of \(n^2+1\), not merely over its prime divisors.
Any direct proof must bridge the gap between “values avoid every fixed finite set of primes” and “infinitely many values have no nontrivial prime divisor.”

literatureSources.title: Infinitely many prime knots with the same Alexander invariants
literatureSources.summary: We revisit the issue of the existence of infinitely many distinct prime knots with the same Alexander invariant. We present infinitely many distinct families, each family made up of infinitely many distinct knots. Within each family, the Alexander invariant is the same. Unlike other examples in the literature, ours are elementary and based on a sub-collection of pretzel knots with three tassels.

literatureSources.title: The polynomials $X^2+(Y^2+1)^2$ and $X^{2} + (Y^3+Z^3)^2$ also capture their primes
literatureSources.summary: We show that there are infinitely many primes of the form $X^2+(Y^2+1)^2$ and $X^2+(Y^3+Z^3)^2$. This extends the work of Friedlander and Iwaniec showing that there are infinitely many primes of the form $X^2+Y^4$. More precisely, Friedlander and Iwaniec obtained an asymptotic formula for the number of primes of this form. For the sequences $X^2+(Y^2+1)^2$ and $X^2+(Y^3+Z^3)^2$ we establish Type II information that is too narrow for an aysmptotic formula, but we can use Harman's sieve method to produce a lower bound of the correct order of magnitude for primes of form $X^2+(Y^2+1)^2$ and $X^2+(Y^3+Z^3)^2$. Estimating the Type II sums is reduced to a counting problem which is solved by using the Weil bound, where the arithmetic input is quite different from the work of Friedlander and Iwaniec for $X^2+Y^4$. We also show that there are infinitely many primes $p=X^2+Y^2$ where $Y$ is represented by an incomplete norm form of degree $k$ with $k-1$ variables. For this we require a Deligne-type bound for correlations of hyper-Kloosterman sums.

literatureSources.title: An elemetary proof of an estimate for a number of primes less than the product of the first $n$ primes
literatureSources.summary: Let $α$ be a real number such that $1< α<2$ and let $x_0=x_0(α)$ be a {\rm(}unique{\rm)} positive solution of the equation $$ x^{α-1} -\fracπ{e^2\sqrt{3}}x +1=0. $$ Then we prove that for each positive integer $n>x_0$ there exist at least $[n^α]$ primes between the $(n+1)$th prime and the product of the first $n+1$ primes. In particular, we establish a recent Cooke's result which asserts that for each positive integer $n$ there are at least $n$ primes between the $(n+1)$th prime and the product of the first $n+1$ primes. Our proof is based on an elementary counting method (enumerative arguments) and the application of Stirling's formula to give upper bound for some binomial coefficients.

literatureSources.title: Two-dimensional magnetic interactions in LaFeAsO
literatureSources.summary: Inelastic neutron scattering measurements demonstrate that the magnetic interactions in antiferromagnetic LaFeAsO are two-dimensional. Spin wave velocities within the Fe layer and the magnitude of the spin gap are similar to the \textit{A}Fe$_2$As$_2$ based materials. However, the ratio of interlayer and intralayer exchange is found to be less than $\sim 10^{-4}$ in LaFeAsO, very similar to the cuprates, and $\sim$ 100 times smaller than that found in \textit{A}Fe$_2$As$_2$ compounds. The results suggest that the effective dimensionality of the magnetic system is highly variable in the parent compounds of the iron arsenides and weak 3-D interactions may limit the maximum attainable superconducting $T_{c}$.

literatureSources.title: Twin Primes In Quadratic Arithmetic Progressions
literatureSources.summary: A recent heuristic argument based on basic concepts in spectral analysis showed that the twin prime conjecture and a few other related primes counting problems are valid. A rigorous version of the spectral method, and a proof for the existence of infinitely many quadratic twin primes $n^{2}+1$ and $n^{2}+3$, $n \geq 1$, are proposed in this note.

literatureSources.title: Infinitely Many Primes (Using Topology)
literatureSources.summary: Problem: Prove there are infinitely many prime numbers. Solution: First recall that an arithmetic progression with difference $ d$ is a sequence of integers $ a_n \subset \mathbb{Z}$ so that for every pair $ a_k, a_{k+1}$ the difference $ a_{k+1} – a_k = d$. We proceed be defining a topology on the set of integers by defining a basis $ B$ of unbounded (in both directions) arithmetic progressions.

literatureSources.summary: Problem: Prove there are infinitely many primes Solution: Denote by $ \pi(n)$ the number of primes less than or equal to $ n$. We will give a lower bound on $ \pi(n)$ which increases without bound as $ n \to \infty$. Note that every number $ n$ can be factored as the product of a square free number $ r$ (a number which no square divides) and a square $ s^2$.

whatWeKnow: If \(n>1\) is odd, then \(n^2+1\equiv 2\pmod 4\), hence composite.
Thus all nontrivial prime examples require \(n\) even.
If an odd prime \(p\mid n^2+1\), then \(-1\) is a quadratic residue mod \(p\), so \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\).
Finite computation checked \(1\le n\le 100\). Prime-producing values were \[ n=1,2,4,6,10,14,16,20,24,26,36,40,54,56,66,74,84,90,94. \] This is finite evidence only, not proof of infinitude.
[source-2] proves related multivariable results, e.g. \[ X^2+(Y^2+1)^2,\qquad X^2+(Y^3+Z^3)^2, \] but these do not imply infinitely many primes \(n^2+1\).
[source-5] directly concerns quadratic progressions, but is recorded only as a proposed/preprint-style claim, not settled proof.
roadblocks: No saved report gives a complete proof of infinitely many primes \(n^2+1\).
The claim that this is a standard open problem is recorded as plausible but not source-backed by the supplied sources.
Multivariable prime-producing theorems have already been rejected as direct routes; do not specialize variables unless a theorem explicitly permits it.
General infinitude of primes is not evidence for infinitude inside \(n^2+1\).
Current computation is bounded and cannot prove an infinite claim.
